edges.relationship: Mazower treats Hobsbawm’s argumentative synthesis and accessible historical writing as a model for the profession.
edges.evidence_note: Own2020review paragraphs on mastery of craft and final paragraph explicitly identify the connection of disparate processes and the model of bringing argument alive. This is a specific methodological resource in Mazower’s retrospective appraisal, not an inferred original formation, apprenticeship, or endorsement of all Hobsbawm’s conclusions. It is newly grounded in his own essay, not a promotion of the inherited2014conference group route.

edges.relationship: Mazower argues that Hobsbawm’s communist loyalties constrained his twentieth-century history while distinguishing this from the value of his Marxist analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Own2020review paragraphs beginning Party membership had affected his work and Unlike his communism. Mazower reports Hobsbawm’s admission to Antonio Polito about avoiding comrades’ sensitivities and calls Age of Extremes a lesser work because it entered that uncomfortable terrain. Praise for Marxism’s crisis analysis, totality and readable synthesis is retained. This is a limited judgment by Mazower, not a claim that every Hobsbawm work is invalid or that the biographies/Polito original were independently read.

edges.relationship: Judt praises Dark Continent but questions how far Europe could have been organized along Nazi lines and how little great-power politics enters its account.
edges.evidence_note: Own1999review final reservations: some democratic attachments persisted despite occupation, and limited attention to international power contributes to exaggerated East/West economic convergence. He expressly calls these minor defects in a confident interpretation. Original1998 and reviewed1999 US manifestation remain distinct; book itself unread. No blanket rejection of Mazower’s anti-teleological argument.

edges.relationship: Judt acknowledges learning especially from Mazower’s writings on recent European history while preparing Postwar.
edges.evidence_note: Own Preface & Acknowledgements in consulted2006 Penguin ebook preview names Harold James, Mark Mazower and Andrew Moravcsik together and says their work leaves an imprint. The individual arrow retains that collective credit and asserts no particular borrowed claim, exclusive influence, or advisor relationship. The whole Postwar body is unread; the acknowledgment is not dated as a new2006formation event merely because this manifestation is consulted.

edges.relationship: Ballinger reports that Mazower finds Foucault’s biopolitical model more useful for studying Nazism than Agamben’s account.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Ballinger2013p.137n.13 states this comparison while citing Mazower’s2008 “Foucault, Agamben: Theory and the Nazis.” No broader Foucault lineage or original formation is asserted. Ballinger’s surrounding argument about DP agency and Arendt is not assigned to Mazower. Underlying Mazower article and complete theoretical texts unread.

edges.relationship: Ballinger identifies Mazower’s objection to the historical precision of Agamben’s account of Nazism.
edges.evidence_note: Named scholarly mediation, Ballinger2013p.137n.13, links Mazower’s2008article to the specific historical-precision criticism and preserves his preference for Foucault. This note does not independently support assigning every nearby criticism of bare life, refugee camps or Arendt to Mazower. The inaccessible original article remains unread; no blanket refutation of Agamben or endorsement of all Foucault is claimed.

edges.relationship: Schwartz identifies Arendt’s rejection of eternal antisemitism as a resource for Mazower’s historically contextual approach.
edges.evidence_note: Named scholarly mediation: Schwartz’s2026review paragraph beginning Even in this more restrained opening section explicitly says Mazower follows Arendt in opposing timeless, inexplicable Jew hatred. Schwartz’s subsequent criticism of Mazower’s handling of Wistrich and continuities remains a substantive held case because Schwartz lacks an endpoint. The resource is specific to the reviewed work, not a global influence claim or an endorsement of all positions in the review; underlying books unread.

edges.relationship: Schwartz compares Mazower’s history of the word antisemitism with Williams’s Keywords as a method of tracing politically charged language.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly undirected named-reader comparison from the opening methodological paragraph of Schwartz’s2026review. The reviewer says Mazower’s project runs along the lines of Keywords; this does not establish direct borrowing or a causal transmission. Schwartz goes on to dispute how the project is executed. No full book reading or claim that both authors share identical politics.

edges.relationship: Jacobson explicitly joins Roediger’s project of placing race at the center of the history of European immigration and assimilation.
edges.evidence_note: Own Whiteness12 names Roediger jointly with KarenBrodkinSacks. Printed17–18 calls Wages of Whiteness important and subtle on political economy, class formation and psychology before identifying limits; actual285/n6–8 identifies the1991 Wages and separately credits other Roediger writing and joint work with JamesBarrett. This positive resource remains distinct from Jacobson’s criticism and does not establish complete agreement or sole influence. Original Roediger works unread.

edges.relationship: Jacobson argues that Roediger’s economic emphasis needs a longer chronology, finer distinctions among forms of whiteness and fuller attention to struggles outside class and labor.
edges.evidence_note: Own17–19 praises Roediger and TheodoreAllen while spelling out three limits: distinctions among white/Caucasian/Celt, historical scale beyond selected decades, and elite or immigrant contests not fully explained by labor interests. Note13 at284 separately includes Roediger among sophisticated writers who sometimes treat Caucasian as unproblematic; that is a different terminological qualification, consolidated here without a duplicate same-pair critique. Jacobson does not reject class/economics or equate European immigrant oppression with AfricanAmerican exclusion (9). Allen retains separate credit; originals unread.

edges.relationship: Jacobson places Higham within an immigration historiography that, in his view, too readily translated earlier European racial distinctions into later ethnic categories.
edges.evidence_note: Own introduction6–9 and actual note13 at284 explain a general historiographic problem and explicitly identify Higham’s Strangers alongside OscarHandlin and MaldwynAllenJones. Jacobson attributes this partly to the subfield’s formation during the consolidation of Caucasian identity, rather than simply ignoring the existence of racial prejudice. This is a bounded criticism of the framework and period categories, not a denial that Higham studied nativism or a refutation of his whole book. Note’s1865–1925 variant is not adopted as bibliography; original Higham book unread.

edges.relationship: Jacobson uses Du Bois’s definition of Blackness through Jim Crow to show how racial classification depends on social power and institutions.
edges.evidence_note: Own printed110, following In Re Halladjian, explicitly turns to DuBois’s Dusk of Dawn and its dialogue on the race concept;301/n45 identifies the1960 Schocken edition of the1940 work,153. Printed124 also connects Schuyler’s account of racial allegiance to DuBois’s psychological-wage formulation, while18 discusses its use through Roediger. This is a specific conceptual resource and reception, not proof Jacobson adopts every DuBois or Roediger claim. Aptheker-edited Against Racism and Black Reconstruction receive distinct references; originals unread.

edges.relationship: Wolfe uses Jacobson’s formulation of republican inclusion and racial/gender exclusion as interdependent to develop his account of race and colonial power.
edges.evidence_note: Own Wolfe2001,875/n29 quotes Jacobson22–23 while discussing Morgan’s slavery/freedom analysis; Morgan and DavidBrionDavis retain separate substantive credit. Wolfe adds a specific reservation about Jacobson’s treatment of liberalism, and893/n100 includes him among resources for the historical expansion of whiteness while preserving differences from anti-Black racialization. Positive use coexists with the separate qualification; original Jacobson22–23 not freshly read, so the quotation’s mediation through Wolfe is explicit.

edges.relationship: Wolfe qualifies Jacobson’s account of republican inclusion and exclusion for leaving liberalism’s own credentials insufficiently interrogated.
edges.evidence_note: Own875/n29 explicitly attaches this limited reservation to his otherwise substantive quotation of Whiteness22–23. This is a brief, scoped critical qualification, not an extended refutation of Jacobson’s book or a claim he ignored all relations of power. Wolfe’s positive use remains separately represented; his893/n100 distinction among racial regimes is not falsely treated as refuting Jacobson’s own9 warning against equating experiences. Original Jacobson22–23 remains unread here.

edges.relationship: Gerstle draws on Jacobson’s account of racialized nationality to situate racial exclusion within the early American republic.
edges.evidence_note: Own Gerstle1999 opening1280 explicitly names MatthewJacobson and RogersSmith for constructions of American nationality present in the Constitution and1790 naturalization rule;note1 identifies Whiteness1998 alongside Smith,Rogin,Roediger,Takaki,Horsman and Higham’s separate resources. This is a specified historiographical use, not sole influence or endorsement of every part of Whiteness. The original book’s22–23 section remains unread here; dated legal interpretations are attributed to the article.

edges.relationship: In Tunc’s comparative account, Jacobson and Bederman extend the study of whiteness into cultural and political histories of racial representation, masculinity and civilization.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation limited to Tunc’s substantive author abstract, which compares Whiteness of a Different Color and Manliness and Civilization, linking archival sources with literary criticism, material culture and gender theory. This is an editorial teaching comparison supported at abstract level, not mutual influence, a shared school or an exclusive origin claim. Full2008 review and complete originals unread in this dossier.

edges.relationship: Uses White’s account of critical history to frame an ethically responsible relation between historical inquiry and educational change (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own382/n1 cites The Burden of History. A specific methodological resource, not endorsement of White’s entire narrative theory or a claim of personal formation. Original essay unread.

edges.relationship: Draws on Dobb’s definition of capitalism through commodified labour power to distinguish capitalist from industrial change (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own391/n20. Katz treats the three-stage model as partly speculative. Marx’s Capital is also cited in the note, but the explicit definition is assigned to Dobb; the original books remain unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Thompson’s analysis of work discipline to connect the habits demanded by industrial work with school-system formation (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own395/n27 names Thompson’s account; Gutman’s Work,Culture and Society is a second cited resource in the same note. No exclusive lineage or full reading of either original essay.

edges.relationship: Applies Davis’s distinction between ideology’s social functions and conscious intentions to popular acceptance of public schooling (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own400/n38–39 uses Davis’s antislavery analysis for the problem of consent. This is an analytical transfer, not a claim that schools and slavery are identical; Katz rejects equating imposition with conspiracy. Davis’s1975book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Uses Gramsci’s distinction between coercion and consent, explicitly through Davis, to analyze the acceptance of public education (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own400/n36 expressly identifies Gramsci as quoted in Davis’s1975bookp349. The mediated route is preserved; Gramsci’s original work and Davis’s book remain unread. Distinct from Davis’s own explanation of ideological functions.

edges.relationship: Uses Scott and Louise Tilly’s joint work among the resources for explaining women’s occupational alternatives and the feminization of teaching (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own389/n18 cites their joint Women’s Work and the Family alongside PatriciaBranca,TheresaMcBride and Katz’s own work. This identifies a bounded contextual resource, not sole authorship or a general Scott influence; LouiseTilly lacks a full endpoint. Cited original essay unread.

edges.relationship: Sugrue recalls Katz’s intellectual inspiration, sustained guidance and support from the period of his dissertation onward.
edges.evidence_note: Own2014memorial reproduced by PennPress: Sugrue describes the poverty-history group, ongoing support and the effect of reading The Undeserving Poor. Not inferred from coediting, appointment or formal supervision; neither the memorial’s1988book date nor the1998collection is assigned as a verified first-publication or causal starting date.

edges.relationship: Makes Du Bois’s research methods and agenda a framework for examining race and the American welfare state (2000).
edges.evidence_note: Authorial abstract expressly states the analytical use. Scope is this article’s declared framework; full body and DuBois originals unread. Does not infer intellectual transmission merely from the1998edited collection’s title.

edges.relationship: Describes population reconstruction from linked census and assessment records as a way to examine social structure and family organization (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own382–383 explains Hamilton research and collaborative extension to Buffalo/ErieCounty. A particular research practice, not sole credit for shared data or a foundation claim. Existing urban and social-history relationships remain distinct.

edges.relationship: Investigates family organization, youth semi-autonomy and household change through the Hamilton research, qualifying the proposed historical pattern (1976).
edges.evidence_note: Own386–388 explicitly calls the semi-autonomy account tenuous and partly speculative. Stern’s2017retrospective769credits Katz,Doucet and Stern’s collaborative family-economy work and the constraints on family strategy. Contribution to a specific research problem, not a settled universal model; original books unread.

edges.relationship: Vovelle identifies Labrousse as the teacher who taught him historical and archival research within a social-history framework.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005answers2–3 and17 explicitly identify Labrousse as his master and explain the passage through economic, conjunctural and social history. Tersen’s referral and the broader Marxist setting retain separate credit. Vovelle subsequently took distance from limits of this framework while keeping social history; no claim of total doctrinal obedience or later individual influence from Simiand simply because a comparison is invoked.

edges.relationship: Vovelle acknowledges Duby’s influence in the development of his history of mentalities.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005answer17 explicitly names the proximity and influence of Georges Duby and Robert Mandrou;2 places the development of this history more with Mandrou/Duby than Braudel. Collective credit is preserved; Duby is not declared sole originator, and inheritance of a research centre alone is not the proof. Mandrou lacks an individual endpoint and is held with the same primary evidence.

edges.relationship: Vovelle uses Braudel’s long-duration account of mentalities to frame the question of change during revolutionary crisis.
edges.evidence_note: Own1991article in2012reprint233–234 explicitly refers jointly to Mandrou’s longer time and Braudel’s long duration, then investigates their relation to abrupt revolutionary mutation. This is a named conceptual starting point, not proof of exclusive formative transmission or a blanket rejection of Braudel. Existing edge_1489 to Annales remains a separate group contribution; it is not retargeted.

edges.relationship: Vovelle names Marx’s writing among the basic reading in his early Marxist historical formation.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005pp1–2 describes an elementary formation through teaching, manuals and basic books, naming La lutte des classes; the surviving idea was a totalizing history connecting economic, social and cultural levels. The transcript supplies no exact Marx edition, and none is invented. Marc Soriano, manuals and translation work are not erased; no claim of advanced Marxology or derivation of every mentalities argument.

edges.relationship: Vovelle recalls using Gramsci in Les jacobins while qualifying how central that reading was to his own research.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005pp6–7 says he exploited Gramsci in Les jacobins (note identifies1999 Les jacobins, de Robespierre à Chevènement) and had earlier assisted Moget with translation work. The latter is recollection, not a substitute translator credit:1959 Oeuvres choisies credits Moget and Armand Monjo, preface Cogniot, per2n2. Vovelle immediately qualifies the usefulness as yes and no; no exclusive or foundational influence claim and no original book read.

edges.relationship: Vovelle regards Gramsci’s transhistorical Jacobinism as historically dated and limits its usefulness for his own historical inquiries.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005p7 follows the acknowledgment of actual use: the transhistorical reading is itself a moment in historical reflection, and its utility for his existing research was yes and no. This specific limitation coexists with a resource arrow and does not reject all Gramsci, deny reading, or establish a contemporary direct exchange.

edges.relationship: Vovelle cites Althusser when describing a flexible economic grounding of total history.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005p7 explicitly says he had read Althusser and refers to the ultimate economic justification while emphasizing flexibility as in Vilar;17 includes Althusser among later reading that brought him something after his path was already formed. Exact Althusser title or edition is not supplied. No original formative influence, rigid economic determinism or equivalence with Vilar’s whole argument is inferred.

edges.relationship: Vovelle treats Ariès’s diverse-source reconstruction of attitudes to death as an exemplary interlocutor for his own inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Own1976pp124 and127 calls the varied-source demonstration brilliant/exemplary and the global model a stimulus to problem formulation;132 calls Ariès his interlocutor and accomplice. Own2005p17 describes Ariès opening avenues in the maturation of a personal approach.1976p124 expressly argues qualitative and serial approaches are complementary; these debts coexist with concrete criticisms. The1974 English essay,1975 French collection and future definitive synthesis remain distinct; no whole book read.

edges.relationship: Vovelle argues that Ariès’s model gives too little explanatory weight to religious and ideological change in attitudes toward death.
edges.evidence_note: Own1976pp129–131 questions material/spiritual reference systems, the privileging of a collective unconscious and idealized tamed origins, and the family explanation of silence in wills. He acknowledges possible overemphasis in his own treatment of Catholic reconquest, accepts some family mediation, and insists his criticism measures the book’s interest. This is a particular methodological disagreement, not a personal denunciation or claim that qualitative sources are invalid;124 explicitly defends complementary methods.

edges.relationship: Darnton reports Ariès’s alternative explanation of Vovelle’s testamentary findings through changed family trust rather than declining religious ritual.
edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation in Darnton1974paragraph beginning Ariès tries to explain Vovelle’s data. This is a precise explanatory alternative, not proof Ariès rejected the archival findings or every dechristianization process. Vovelle’s own1976p131 acknowledges disagreement on this family explanation while sharing the importance of family mediation. Ariès’s underlying work remains unread; Darnton’s report is not silently promoted to a freshly read Ariès passage.

edges.relationship: Darnton praises Vovelle’s testamentary research but questions whether declining ritual proves dechristianization and how fully the change is explained.
edges.evidence_note: Own1974review final paragraphs distinguish decline from extinction and suggest that abandoning baroque rites could signify religious purification. He also finds socio-economic change too general and some explanation circular, while praising the method as a major historical advance and acknowledging similar explanatory limits in other great theses. This is not a rejection of quantitative research or proof Vovelle asserted Christianity vanished; original monograph unread.

edges.relationship: Vovelle explicitly shares Delumeau’s emphasis on inherited magical thought in early modern religious behavior.
edges.evidence_note: Own1976p122 states agreement on the weight of magical belief and ritual while discussing a justified criticism of Mourir autrefois and the difficulty of recovering practices from sources. The unnamed critic is not automatically Delumeau. This specific reverse resource differs from existing edge_2036 Vovelle-to-Delumeau and undirected methodological dialogue edge_2037; neither is duplicated or withdrawn. No claim of identical religious interpretations or whole-book reading.

edges.relationship: Vovelle opposes reducing revolutionary history to an ideological history of texts and discourse associated with Furet.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005pp14–15 frames his defense of total/global revolutionary history against what he describes as the Furet universe of ideological texts and discourse. He recognizes a conjunctural political dimension to his own bicentenary posture and also claims a wider opening of research; this is Vovelle’s retrospective characterization, not a neutral description of all Furet works. He reports an earlier critique of L’Atelier de l’histoire at11 but that review and the original Furet book are not read. No automatic reciprocal Furet-to-Vovelle arrow.

edges.relationship: Vovelle compares his later encounter with Ginzburg to discovering historians independently posing simultaneous problems.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005p17 describes discovery through parallel problem setting rather than a formative chance encounter;8–9 separately recognizes Italian/Ginzburg case-study initiatives while recalling US reception of his own work. This is an undirected methodological comparison, not evidence Ginzburg caused Vovelle’s established approach, that he read every microhistorical work, or that their methods coincide in full.

edges.relationship: Winter challenges Ferguson’s confident counterfactual account of British nonintervention in1914 as exceeding the available evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Distinguishes projections from predictions and offers a defensive-war alternative. Praises economic, morale and surrender chapters. Ferguson disputes this reading in the reply.

edges.relationship: Ferguson rejects Winter’s German-war-economy explanation and argues that Winter’s causal judgments themselves require counterfactuals.
edges.evidence_note: Own reply contests Winter’s interpretation, including victory timing and stabilization. This is Ferguson’s attributed position; no book verification claimed.

edges.relationship: Foner criticizes Colossus for presenting a sanitized account of American continental expansion that underplays military conquest.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005 review explicitly names Colossus and contrasts Ferguson’s brief account with Fred Anderson and Andrew Cayton’s coauthored Dominion of War. Criticism targets the account’s impression of peaceful settlement and land purchase, not a claim that Ferguson denies all American empire. Foner’s later criticisms of Dominion’s biography structure, slavery omissions and internal roots are not reassigned to Ferguson. Original books unread.

edges.relationship: Ferguson takes Weber’s Protestant-ethic thesis as a framework for examining the relationship between religion and economic development.
edges.evidence_note: Own adapted2011 excerpt47 explains the thesis and48 retains a qualified positive argument about Protestant literacy, trust, saving and human capital. Its final reformulation emphasizes the word ethic. Substantial criticism coexists with this conceptual use: no complete assent, direct mentorship, or unqualified religious superiority claim inferred. Weber’s original essays and full Civilization unread.

edges.relationship: Ferguson criticizes Weber’s evidence and causal account while retaining a qualified relationship between Protestantism and economic development.
edges.evidence_note: Own48 identifies tensions in rational/irrational asceticism, Weber’s treatment of Jewish capitalism, overlooked Catholic entrepreneurs and inadequate comparative evidence. He then presents Tawney’s causal objection and an unnamed city study, before offering literacy/human-capital mechanisms. This is partial revision, not rejection of every Weberian proposition; neither unnamed study nor Tawney is falsely credited as Ferguson’s discovery. Originals unread.

edges.relationship: Ferguson cites Tawney’s challenge to treating religious doctrine as the prior cause of capitalist economic behavior.
edges.evidence_note: Own48 explicitly singles out R.H.Tawney among later scholars questioning Weber’s causal direction, then discusses pre-Reformation capitalist developments and anti-capitalist reformers. This is a named critical resource within Ferguson’s qualified argument; no exact Tawney title, edition or original passage supplied by the excerpt, and none invented. Tawney’s original unread.

edges.relationship: In Mähkä and Tringham’s account, Ferguson counters Thompson’s dismissal of counterfactual history by defending alternatives grounded in contemporary evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive scholarly mediation: their Ferguson section reports Thompson among several critics cited in the1997 Introduction4–6 and presents Ferguson’s restricted plausible-alternatives argument85–89. He also criticizes frivolous and anachronistic scenarios12–20. This is a methodological disagreement, not a personal exchange or claim Thompson reviewed Ferguson; originals and original wording context unread. Carr,Croce and Oakeshott retain separate credit and missing-endpoint dispositions.
